intro: The second movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 4 is marked In gemächlicher Bewegung. Ohne Hast. The solo violin is tuned a whole tone high to sound like a rough country fiddle and plays a lopsided dance, which a warmer Ländler interrupts twice.

sections.label: A · Horn call, then solo violin
sections.mNote: The solo violin’s strings are tuned a whole tone high.

sections.label: B · F major Ländler for woodwinds
sections.mNote: A Ländler over held horns and plucked basses.

sections.label: A′ · The fiddle returns
sections.mNote: The strings tap with the wood of their bows.

sections.label: B′ · Second trio, woodwind dance theme
sections.mNote: The second trio is longer and moves through major keys.

sections.label: A″ · Dance returns, muted strings
sections.mNote: Soft horns and harp accompany the last quick figures.

cues.title: Solo violin tuned a tone high
cues.text: After the horn opening, the solo violin enters with its strings tuned a whole tone above their usual pitch. Mahler marked it to sound like a fiddle, played forcefully. Muted solo viola and cello play beneath it.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 275: horn opening, solo violin wie eine Fidel, muted solo viola and cello. The footnote requires a violin tuned a whole tone high. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bruno Walter’s title, 1901
cues.text: Bruno Walter gave this fiddler a name: “Freund Hein Strikes Up the Dance”. Freund Hein is Death. Walter passed on the title in a letter to Ludwig Schiedermair of 5 December 1901, written at Mahler’s request.
cues.evidence: Bruno Walter to Ludwig Schiedermair, 5 December 1901, written at Mahler’s request and quoted by Bettie Jo Basinger: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: First trio in F major
cues.text: The first trio is in F major. Oboes and clarinets take over the dance, over held horn notes and pizzicato basses. The solo violin rests.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 280–283, rehearsal 3 onwards; woodwind trio over horns and pizzicato bass. F-major trio identified in Basinger’s guide: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Manuscript leaf for Arnold Rosé, 1902
cues.text: On 11 January 1902, the day before the Vienna performance, Mahler gave the violinist Arnold Rosé a manuscript leaf of this solo. In that draft the solo violin is tuned a half-tone high. The printed score asks for a whole tone.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes the manuscript (solo violin “um einen halben Ton höher gestimmt”), given to Arnold Rosé the day before the Vienna premiere, with the final tuning a whole tone higher: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/ . The Vienna concert date, 12 January 1902, is on its history page: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-history/

cues.title: End of the first trio
cues.text: The first trio stays in F major to the end. Low strings play softly and horns hold pppp-bound stopped notes; Mahler marks morendo as the dynamic falls to pppp before the scherzo returns.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 283, rehearsal 4: morendo in the low strings, stopped horns and pppp: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the scherzo, C minor
cues.text: At rehearsal 5 (Tempo I) the scherzo returns in C minor. This time Mahler marks the solo violin leidenschaftlich (passionate). The second violins play col legno, with the wood of the bow, and the first horn is marked sehr hervortretend, very prominent.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 284, rehearsal 5: Tempo I, solo violin leidenschaftlich, second violins col legno, first horn sehr hervortretend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alma Mahler’s claim about Böcklin
cues.text: Alma Mahler later claimed that Arnold Böcklin’s Self-Portrait with Death Fiddling (1872), in which a skeleton plays into the painter’s ear, inspired this scherzo. She and Mahler had not yet met when he wrote it. He did admire Böcklin.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger records Alma’s claim, the picture’s composition, Mahler’s fondness for Böcklin and the fact that the couple had not met: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation page reports Alma’s account: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/

cues.title: Second trio
cues.text: The woodwinds return to the trio’s dance. The trio is longer than at its first appearance, with lyrical digressions in its major-key phrases, before the music of the solo violin returns.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the second trio’s enlarged form and lyrical digressions: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second trio in D major
cues.text: The trio moves to D major. The clarinets play the melody over harp arpeggios, the violins play with portamento, and a contrabassoon doubles the double basses.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 295–297, the second trio’s D-major expansion, clarinet melody, violin portamento, harp and contrabassoon doubling the bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Contrabassoon added in proof
cues.text: The contrabassoon doubling the double basses in bars 246–51 was not in Mahler’s original scoring. He added it in the proofs. The plate had no room for another staff, so the published score labels one line “Ctrfag. u. Cb. unisono”.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s catalogue of the Fourth Symphony’s printed sources describes the proof revision in bars 246–51 and the engraver’s solution: http://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph4/Symph4prints.htm

cues.title: Return of Tempo I
cues.text: The opening tempo returns over pizzicato cellos and basses. Muted violins and violas play their figures at ppp, horns hold soft chords and piccolos add small ornaments.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 299, rehearsal 13: Tempo I, muted strings sempre ppp, pizzicato cellos and basses, horn chords, harp and piccolos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Into the first trio in F major
transitions.from: A · Horn call, then solo violin
transitions.to: B · F major Ländler for woodwinds
transitions.how: The C minor scherzo is followed by the first trio, in F major. The oboe holds a note and the clarinet plays a figure over sustained horn harmony, and the basses play the beat pizzicato. At Etwas gemächlicher Mahler slows the tempo, and the solo violin stops playing.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 280, rehearsal 3 and Etwas gemächlicher; F-major trio identified in https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Return of the solo violin in C minor
transitions.from: B · F major Ländler for woodwinds
transitions.how: The trio dies away and the score returns to Tempo I. Muted inner strings start moving first. The solo violin then re-enters in C minor, now marked leidenschaftlich. A prominent horn part and second violins playing col legno go with the return.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 283–284, rehearsal 5 and the solo violin’s leidenschaftlich entry.

transitions.title: Trilling woodwinds bring back the Ländler
transitions.to: B′ · Second trio, woodwind dance theme
transitions.how: The scherzo’s busy string writing stops as the trio returns. Flutes and oboes trill over sustained horns and trumpets, and harp and glockenspiel add bright touches. The familiar major-key dance comes back in expanded form and is given more time than before.
transitions.evidence: Full score, second trio, printed pp. 291–298; expanded trio described in https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Return to Tempo I with muted strings
transitions.from: B′ · Second trio, woodwind dance theme
transitions.how: The enlarged trio slows and thins before Tempo I returns. Cellos and basses play pizzicato beneath figures in the muted violins and violas, marked ppp. Horns hold the harmony, and harp and piccolos add short accents to the returning dance.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 298–299, reaching rehearsal 13.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, II. In gemächlicher Bewegung, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Second movement, printed pp. 275–303, rehearsal figures 1–14: high-tuned solo violin, two woodwind trios and the muted closing dance.

timeline.note: A horn plays above soft woodwind trills; the high-tuned violin follows over muted viola and cello solos.
Violins, violas and basses accompany the fiddle with muted and pizzicato figures, with timpani and low winds.
Woodwinds lead the first trio over held horns and plucked basses, with trills and harp.
Cellos and basses play quietly beneath held horns as the trio fades to pppp.
The scherzo returns. The solo violin plays over horns, harp, bass drum and strings that tap col legno.
Muted trumpet, cymbals and timpani join the fiddle and the busy strings.
Muted horns and trumpets and a glockenspiel punctuate the strings.
Flutes, piccolos and oboes trill above held brass notes; glockenspiel and harp play in the second trio.
In D major clarinets play, violins slide, harp arpeggiates and contrabassoon doubles the basses.
The trio swells and holds, with piccolo and flutes above divided strings, before the tempo begins to return.
Muted violins and violas play at ppp over plucked cellos and basses, with held horns, harp and piccolo.
Woodwind trills, triangle, harp and tam-tam play over muted strings.
Cellos slide on the C string over soft basses while the clarinets die away.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
